howTo.name: Dim Ambient Room Lighting
howTo.text: For accurate near-black OLED and Mini-LED blooming evaluation, perform testing in a darkened room without direct screen reflections.

howTo.name: Select Test Pattern
howTo.text: Choose from the Grayscale Gradient, 5% Near-Black Field, Starfield Blooming, or Peak Highlight Clipping.

howTo.name: Activate Fullscreen Mode
howTo.text: Click Fullscreen to expand the pattern to the physical edges of your display panel, hiding browser UI elements.

howTo.name: Audit Display Uniformity
howTo.text: Inspect the panel for visible vertical stripes, color tinting across corners, or haloing around high-contrast star elements.

faq.q: What causes color banding on modern gaming monitors and TVs?
faq.a: Color banding occurs when a display cannot render subtle tonal transitions smoothly. Panels with 8-bit color depth only have 256 shades per RGB channel (16.7 million total colors). When rendering high-dynamic-range content without spatial/temporal dithering (FRC), visible stair-stepping artifacts appear across gradients.

faq.q: What is the 5% gray test and why is it standard for OLEDs?
faq.a: OLED subpixels produce perfect zero-nit blacks when turned off. However, transitioning subpixels from pure black to just above black (1% to 5% luminance) is where manufacturing variations in thin-film transistors (TFTs) become visible, manifesting as subtle vertical stripes or panel vignetting.

Mini-LED displays use localized full-array backlights divided into hundreds or thousands of physical dimming zones. When a small bright object (such as a star in space or white text) appears against a deep black background, light spills into adjacent pixels within the same dimming zone, creating a noticeable halo or 'blooming' effect.

A native 10-bit panel has hardware registers to display 1,024 shades per channel (1.07 billion colors). An '8-bit + FRC' (Frame Rate Control) panel uses rapid temporal pixel flickering between two adjacent 8-bit shades to simulate intermediate colors, which can sometimes produce subtle crawling noise in dark gray gradients.

toolHtml:
Pattern: 10-Bit Grayscale Gradient • Click canvas for Fullscreen
What to Look For: Gradient Banding

Observe the smooth ramp from pure black to peak white. If distinct vertical vertical 'steps' or harsh color lines appear, your panel is either restricted to 8-bit color or applying heavy temporal FRC dithering.

What to Look For: 5% OLED Gray

In a dark room, verify that the 5% gray field is uniform across the entire surface. Watch for vertical 'prison bar' banding, vignetting along outer edges, or pink/yellow color tints.

What to Look For: Mini-LED Blooming

Evaluate the perimeter around bright stars on the black background. Noticeable blue or white glowing halos indicate the physical boundaries of your television's local dimming zones.
articleHtml:
HDR Display Architecture: EOTF PQ Curves, 10-Bit Color Depth, and Panel Uniformity

High Dynamic Range video fundamentally expands both peak specular highlight luminance and color volume. Achieving calibrated HDR playback requires understanding electro-optical transfer functions, bit depth constraints, and dark-room panel characteristics.

The SMPTE ST 2084 Perceptual Quantizer (PQ) Curve

Traditional Standard Dynamic Range (SDR) relies on power-law gamma curves (Gamma 2.2 / 2.4) designed for legacy cathode-ray tubes capped at 100 nits. High Dynamic Range standardizes on the SMPTE ST 2084 Perceptual Quantizer (PQ):

$$L = 10,000 \times \left( \frac{\max(N^{1/m_2} - c_1, 0)}{c_2 - c_3 N^{1/m_2}} \right)^{1/m_1}$$

Unlike relative gamma curves, PQ is an absolute luminance curve defining brightness up to 10,000 nits. If a display has a physical peak of 800 nits (standard on LG and Sony WOLED televisions [Confirmed: RTINGS Display Benchmarks]), any input metadata exceeding 800 nits must either be clipped or compressed using tone mapping.

Color Banding and 8-Bit + FRC Dithering

To display the Rec. 2020 and DCI-P3 color spaces without visible stair-stepping, 10 bits per RGB channel is mandatory ($2^{10} = 1,024\text{ quantization levels}$). Commercial displays commonly adopt one of two approaches:

  • Native 10-Bit Silicon: Direct 10-bit physical driver ICs capable of rendering all 1.07 billion colors natively without temporal modulation.
  • 8-Bit + FRC (Frame Rate Control): An 8-bit panel that modulates subpixels between adjacent colors over successive refresh frames at 60Hz or 120Hz. While cost-effective, FRC can introduce subtle temporal noise or micro-banding across wide, slow gradients.

OLED Near-Black Uniformity and 5% Gray Fields

At 0% video signal level, OLED subpixels receive zero electrical current, providing an infinite contrast ratio. However, driving organic semiconductor diodes at low currents (1% to 5% luminance) requires precise voltage thresholds. Subpixel manufacturing variations across large substrate motherglass sheets can produce subtle vertical banding lines (often nicknamed 'jailbars') or edge vignetting.

Calibration Notice: Pattern generation in browser canvas is calibrated to system sRGB and Display P3 color spaces. For hardware-level studio calibration, professional signal generators are recommended. ToolkitGen is an independent platform.
